report:
Conclusion: the claim is **not false as a population-level average**, but it is often overstated. In chronic inflammatory conditions, randomized-trial meta-analyses report that anti-cytokine/anti-inflammatory treatment produces a **small-to-moderate reduction in depressive symptoms versus placebo**, with substantial heterogeneity and limits. A focused review of anti-cytokine trials in chronic inflammatory conditions was designed precisely to test antidepressant activity (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/). A broader JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis found anti-inflammatory treatment reduced depressive symptoms (SMD −0.34; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.11) but with very high heterogeneity (I²=90%) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25322082/). An Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases abstract reported anti-IL-6 benefit persisted after adjustment for disease activity (SMD=0.25, p=0.03), suggesting the effect is not merely “feeling better because arthritis improved” (https://ard.bmj.com/content/76/Suppl_2/250.2).

Important boundary: in primary treatment-resistant major depression, infliximab was not broadly effective; benefit appeared concentrated in high-baseline-inflammation subgroups (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1356541). So the evidence supports a modest, inflammation-linked antidepressant effect in some patients—not a universal depression treatment, and not proof every anti-cytokine helps every patient.
